headlines.article_text: SpaceX rival Eutelsat up 19% as Ukraine's Starshield limits raise fears Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Eutelsat soared again on Friday after competitor SpaceX's Starlink systems came under criticism. Ukrainian officials said the system, which is critical to its defense against Russian attacks, was restricted. Eutelsat is known as Europe's answer to SpaceX and aims to challenge its market dominance. In this article E3B-DE SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A satellite dish in a ground network of satellites at Eutelsat's Madeira office. Photographer: /Bloomberg via Getty Images Zed Jameson | Bloomberg via Getty Images Shares of French Satellite Group Eutelsat soared this week as SpaceX 's Starshield drew criticism after the Ukrainian military's access to its systems was suddenly restricted. Earlier this week, tensions rose between the U.S. and Ukraine after Kyiv accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink internet service without warning, curbing connectivity and limiting Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the U.S., saying "Starlink was switched off" in the middle of the night, preventing Ukrainian drones from intercepting Russian attacks, and ultimately contributing to civilian deaths. "They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said. "It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work." SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded by shifting blame on the U.S. government and said that Starshield systems were under Washington and President Donald Trump's control. Eutelsat shares rose 19% on Friday, and was up 25% over the past five days following the news of Starlink's struggles in Ukraine. Eutelsat shares over the past five days. Eutelsat's share move this week is more evidence "supporting the sovereign value of European Satellite networks," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Thursday. Markets viewed Eutelsat as "the credible Starlink alternative" amid the disruption, they added. "Whilst we note Eutelsat does offer a global LEO [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we believe it lacks the scale to offer the number of terminals that Starlink can provide," they added. "We would expect the shares to give up some of the gains." Eutelsat consolidated with satellite internet provider OneWeb in 2023, looking to challenge Starlink's market dominance. However, Eutelsat currently has over 600 satellites in orbit, while Starlink has more than 6,750, the company's websites show. Ukraine's deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure, and transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Friday that Russia had amped up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, taking advantage of restrictions on military applications, including striking bridges, railway networks, and border crossings. "With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said. "We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day. headlines.article_text: Tesla Roadster reveal: What to know about the delayed EV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster from a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday. CEO Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. Tesla said the new Roadster, equipped with SpaceX thrusters, can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second. In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 8:08 08:08 Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster, showing off its flying-car ambitions Squawk Box Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering. "You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. Tesla | Via Reuters The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company. At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground. The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience. Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026 Source: Tesla Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly." The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics. One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver. watch now VIDEO 4:03 04:03 Dan Ives on Tesla stocks: A big step in the right direction Closing Bell Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." After the event, O'Connor said what he saw was "off the charts." Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday. headlines.summary: KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants.
headlines.article_text: KFC to switch from Pepsi to Coca-Cola in 2027 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants. The fried chicken chain has served Pepsi drinks ever since the food and beverage giant acquired KFC in 1986. KFC is trying to win back U.S. diners who have ditched its buckets for rivals such as Chick-fil-A. In this article YUM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:45 01:45 KFC to switch to Coca-Cola drinks in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades Squawk Box KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday. Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast. The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us." Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum Brands KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, Jan. 29, 2021. Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty Images For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House , its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks. KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said. Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets. For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway , the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express. headlines.title: Norway's $2 trillion wealth fund was frozen out of major defense companies. That may be about to change
headlines.summary: Existing ethical rules mean the fund is not permitted to invest in companies like Lockheed Martin and Boeing.
headlines.article_text: Norway wealth fund may soon be allowed to invest in defense giants Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Proposed changes to Norway's sovereign wealth fund ethics rules could open the door to investments in more Western defense companies. The fund is currently barred from investing in companies including Lockheed Martin and Boeing because of their involvement in nuclear weapons production. Norway will consult on the proposals before the government puts forward a new ethics framework, with parliament expected to vote on the changes in mid-2027. A BAE Systems Hawk T1 jet, pictured Sept. 20, 2026. BAE Systems has been excluded from NBIM's fund since 2018. Artur Widak | Nurphoto | Getty Images Norway's $2.3 trillion oil fund could soon invest in Western defense companies after years of being frozen out of much of the sector by state ethics guidelines. The sovereign wealth fund is currently worth around 21.8 trillion Norwegian kroner, or $2.3 trillion, making it the largest fund of its kind in the world. With stakes in around 1.5% of the world's publicly listed companies, the fund is one of the biggest investors in the stock market worldwide. In November 2025, a review was ordered into the ethical guidelines governing how Norges Bank invests, following controversy over divestments from some Israeli and American firms. On Thursday, the independent Gjedrem Committee submitted the review's findings to the Norwegian Ministry of Finance. It included a recommendation for radical change to the fund's approach to defense investments, arguing that "Norges Bank must be prepared for situations where conflicts escalate into war." Current ethical rules prohibit the fund from making investments in companies including Airbus , BAE Systems , Boeing , BWX Technologies and Lockheed Martin , as they contribute to the manufacturing of nuclear weapons. The fund does hold some defense stocks, including a 2.3% stake in Germany's Rheinmetall , and a 1.5% stake in Italy's Leonardo . The Gjedrem Committee said Thursday that although the nuclear weapons criterion should be retained, "its scope should change." "The Fund is not to be invested in companies that produce nuclear weapons, unless the company is domiciled in a nuclear-weapon state under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that is allied with Norway," it said in its report. "Several European and American companies that produce components for nuclear weapons can therefore be reincluded." It added that potential investment should include companies producing weapons that Norway needs for its own defense, and proposed removing the requirement for arms-makers to be assessed for whether their products are being used by nations in accordance with international humanitarian law. The committee noted that alongside rising geopolitical instability, wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, and energy security concerns, the fund's capital and influence meant it was "timely to reassess the ethical framework." "The Fund's size and reach give better access to company management and boards than the Fund had in 2003," it said. "In a time of a more demanding political situation abroad, this provides opportunities of which the management should make use." "The liberal, rules-based international order is in decline," it added. "Economic policies are increasingly used as instruments of foreign policy. Cooperation between countries has become more transactional and negotiation-driven in recent years." It warned that in this environment, other governments can "more readily perceive ethically motivated exclusions as the policy of the Norwegian government." Norway's oil fund was set up in the 1990s to invest revenues from the country's oil and gas industry. While Norway's finance ministry and central bank are involved in the governance of the fund, investment decisions are made by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), with exclusion recommendations historically put forward by its independent Council on Ethics. "There have been reactions and threats of countermeasures," the Gjedrem Committee said in its report on Thursday. "Retaliatory measures could hit the Fund and other Norwegian interests." U.S. backlash In September last year, the U.S. State Department told CNBC it was "very troubled" by NBIM's decision to exit positions in American machinery manufacturer Caterpillar and five Israeli banks, accusing the fund of basing its decision on "illegitimate claims." NBIM had cited "unacceptable risk" that the companies were contributing to rights violations in Palestinian territories when it divested. Norway's finance minister, Jens Stoltenberg – former secretary general of NATO – said at the time that it was "not a political decision." The Gjedrem Committee noted on Thursday that the risk of further backlash to NBIM's investment choices was also rising as public finances came under greater pressure in many countries. "High government debt can jeopardize economic stability in countries, but can also give an incentive to look to foreign investors' interest and dividend income as a revenue base for the state," it warned. The committee members concluded that although the guidelines underpinning the fund's ethical framework still have broad support, they had come under pressure against the political backdrop. "The conditions for exercising ownership have become more restrictive, in the U.S. among other places," they said. The Gjedrem Committee recommended that the Council on Ethics should continue to operate, but that it should no longer advise NBIM on taking action over ethical concerns. Instead, it should be limited to delivering analysis on breaches of the ethical guidelines by companies, the committee added. No new companies will immediately be included in or excluded from the fund's portfolio as a result of the report's recommendations – but the recommendations pave the way for the fund to invest in some American and European defense companies that are currently barred under the fund's ethics rules. Norway will now hold a public consultation on the recommendations made in the report, with the central bank due to submit its response in January. The finance ministry will propose a new ethics framework in a white paper in the spring, with Norway's parliament expected to vote on the changes in mid-2027. Until then, the fund's current ethical guidelines and exclusion framework remain unchanged. "The Council on Ethics has just received the Gjedrem Committee's report," Svein Richard Brandtzæg, chair of the wealth fund's Council on Ethics, said in an emailed statement on Thursday morning. "We will study the report carefully. We will then hold thorough discussions within the Council and submit our response in the upcoming public consultation." Until November 2025, the Executive Board of Norges Bank decided whether companies should be excluded from the fund's investment portfolio or placed on an observation list. These decisions were informed by the Council on Ethics, an independent body appointed by Norway's Ministry of Finance. But, pending the Gjedrem Committee's review, temporary guidelines were put in place, under which Norges Bank could no longer make those decisions. The temporary guidelines stipulated that the board may only revoke previous decisions on excluding a company or putting it on the observation list. Meanwhile, the Council on Ethics was stripped of its ability to recommend observation or exclusion at least until the ethical framework review is finalized. The temporary guidelines will remain in place until the 2027 parliamentary vote on the Gjedrem Committee's review. 'Other investors pay attention' The Gjedrem Committee's report was met with backlash from some human rights groups, who argued decisions made in Norway could have implications for international investment trends.
